claim: Conditional loss of the de novo DNA methyltransferase Dnmt3a in mouse excitatory neurons altered expression of synapse-related genes.
source: We found that conditional loss of the de novo DNA methyltransferase Dnmt3a in mouse excitatory neurons altered expression of synapse-related genes, stunted synapse maturation, and impaired working memory and social interest.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from RNA-seq showing differentially expressed genes (Figure 3A-B) and behavioral tests (Figure 1C-E).

claim: Conditional loss of Dnmt3a in mouse excitatory neurons stunted synapse maturation.
source: We found that conditional loss of the de novo DNA methyltransferase Dnmt3a in mouse excitatory neurons altered expression of synapse-related genes, stunted synapse maturation, and impaired working memory and social interest.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing dendritic spine morphology changes (Figure 2A-D) and electrophysiological measurements (Figure 2E-I).

claim: Conditional loss of Dnmt3a in mouse excitatory neurons impaired working memory.
source: We found that conditional loss of the de novo DNA methyltransferase Dnmt3a in mouse excitatory neurons altered expression of synapse-related genes, stunted synapse maturation, and impaired working memory and social interest.
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data from Y-maze tests showing reduced spontaneous alternations (Figure 1C).

claim: Conditional loss of Dnmt3a in mouse excitatory neurons impaired social interest.
source: We found that conditional loss of the de novo DNA methyltransferase Dnmt3a in mouse excitatory neurons altered expression of synapse-related genes, stunted synapse maturation, and impaired working memory and social interest.
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data from three-chamber sociability tests showing reduced time spent with novel mice (Figure 1D).

claim: Loss of Dnmt3a abolished postnatal accumulation of CG DNA methylation in adult neurons.
source: At the genomic level, loss of Dnmt3a abolished postnatal accumulation of CG and non-CG DNA methylation, leaving adult neurons with an unmethylated, fetal-like epigenomic pattern at ~222,000 genomic regions.
evidence: This claim is supported by MethylC-seq data showing reduced mCG levels in P39 cKO neurons (Figure 3C).

claim: Loss of Dnmt3a abolished postnatal accumulation of non-CG DNA methylation in adult neurons.
source: At the genomic level, loss of Dnmt3a abolished postnatal accumulation of CG and non-CG DNA methylation, leaving adult neurons with an unmethylated, fetal-like epigenomic pattern at ~222,000 genomic regions.
evidence: This claim is supported by MethylC-seq data showing eliminated mCH in P39 cKO neurons (Figure 3C).

claim: Loss of Dnmt3a left adult neurons with an unmethylated, fetal-like epigenomic pattern at approximately 222,000 genomic regions.
source: At the genomic level, loss of Dnmt3a abolished postnatal accumulation of CG and non-CG DNA methylation, leaving adult neurons with an unmethylated, fetal-like epigenomic pattern at ~222,000 genomic regions.
evidence: This claim is supported by identification of 222,006 differentially methylated regions (DMRs) in P39 cKO neurons (Figure 3F-H and Supplementary file 3).

claim: The PRC2-associated histone modification, H3K27me3, increased at many sites following loss of Dnmt3a.
source: The PRC2-associated histone modification, H3K27me3, increased at many of these sites.
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP-seq data showing 4040 regions with significantly increased H3K27me3 in P39 cKO neurons (Figure 4B-D and Supplementary file 7).

claim: DNA methylation and polycomb repressive complex 2 (PRC2) regulate neuronal development and function.
source: Two epigenetic pathways of transcriptional repression, DNA methylation and polycomb repressive complex 2 (PRC2), are known to regulate neuronal development and function.
evidence: This claim is based on established scientific knowledge as indicated by the use of 'are known to'.

claim: Neurons accumulate a substantial amount of non-CG methylation (mCH) during postnatal brain development in the first 2-3 weeks of life in mice.
source: While mC primarily occurs at CG dinucleotides (mCG) in mammalian tissues, neurons also accumulate a substantial amount of non-CG methylation (mCH) during postnatal brain development in the first 2–3 weeks of life in mice and the first two decades in humans (Lister et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work (Lister et al., 2013).

claim: Neurons accumulate a substantial amount of non-CG methylation (mCH) during postnatal brain development in the first two decades in humans.
source: While mC primarily occurs at CG dinucleotides (mCG) in mammalian tissues, neurons also accumulate a substantial amount of non-CG methylation (mCH) during postnatal brain development in the first 2–3 weeks of life in mice and the first two decades in humans (Lister et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work (Lister et al., 2013).

claim: Accumulation of mCH depends on the activity of the de novo DNA methyltransferase DNMT3A.
source: Accumulation of mCH, and the gain of mCG at specific sites, depend on the activity of the de novo DNA methyltransferase DNMT3A (Gabel et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work (Gabel et al., 2015).

claim: The gain of mCG at specific sites depends on the activity of the de novo DNA methyltransferase DNMT3A.
source: Accumulation of mCH, and the gain of mCG at specific sites, depend on the activity of the de novo DNA methyltransferase DNMT3A (Gabel et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work (Gabel et al., 2015).

claim: The abundance of Dnmt3a mRNA peaks during the second postnatal week in mice.
source: In mice, the abundance of Dnmt3a mRNA and protein peaks during the second postnatal week (Lister et al., 2013; Stroud et al., 2017), a time of intense synaptogenesis and neuronal maturation.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work (Lister et al., 2013; Stroud et al., 2017).

claim: The abundance of Dnmt3a protein peaks during the second postnatal week in mice.
source: In mice, the abundance of Dnmt3a mRNA and protein peaks during the second postnatal week (Lister et al., 2013; Stroud et al., 2017), a time of intense synaptogenesis and neuronal maturation.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work (Lister et al., 2013; Stroud et al., 2017).

claim: The second postnatal week in mice is a time of intense synaptogenesis and neuronal maturation.
source: In mice, the abundance of Dnmt3a mRNA and protein peaks during the second postnatal week (Lister et al., 2013; Stroud et al., 2017), a time of intense synaptogenesis and neuronal maturation.
evidence: This claim is based on established scientific knowledge about mouse brain development.

claim: Deleting Dnmt3a around embryonic day 7.5 (E7.5) driven by the Nestin promoter dramatically impaired neuromuscular and cognitive development.
source: Deleting Dnmt3a around embryonic day 7.5 (E7.5) driven by the Nestin promoter dramatically impaired neuromuscular and cognitive development and led to early death (Nguyen et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work (Nguyen et al., 2007).

claim: Deleting Dnmt3a around embryonic day 7.5 (E7.5) driven by the Nestin promoter led to early death.
source: Deleting Dnmt3a around embryonic day 7.5 (E7.5) driven by the Nestin promoter dramatically impaired neuromuscular and cognitive development and led to early death (Nguyen et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work (Nguyen et al., 2007).

claim: Early loss of Dnmt3a specifically affects the expression of long genes with high levels of gene body mCA.
source: This early loss of Dnmt3a specifically affects the expression of long genes with high levels of gene body mCA (Boxer et al., 2020; Kinde et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work (Boxer et al., 2020; Kinde et al., 2016).

claim: Deletion of Dnmt3a starting around postnatal day 14 driven by the Camk2a promoter caused few behavioral or electrophysiological phenotypes.
source: By contrast, deletion of Dnmt3a starting around postnatal day 14 driven by the Camk2a promoter caused few behavioral or electrophysiological phenotypes (Feng et al., 2010), with only subtle alterations in learning and memory depending on genetic background (Morris et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work (Feng et al., 2010; Morris et al., 2014).

claim: Deletion of Dnmt3a starting around postnatal day 14 driven by the Camk2a promoter caused only subtle alterations in learning and memory depending on genetic background.
source: By contrast, deletion of Dnmt3a starting around postnatal day 14 driven by the Camk2a promoter caused few behavioral or electrophysiological phenotypes (Feng et al., 2010), with only subtle alterations in learning and memory depending on genetic background (Morris et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work (Morris et al., 2014).

claim: Dnmt3a may play a critical role during a specific time window between late gestation and early postnatal life.
source: These results suggest that Dnmt3a may play a critical role during a specific time window between late gestation and early postnatal life.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the contrasting results of Dnmt3a deletion at different developmental time points.

claim: Regulated gains and losses of DNA methylation throughout the genome establish unique epigenomic signatures of neuronal cell types during late gestation and early postnatal life.
source: During these developmental stages, regulated gains and losses of DNA methylation throughout the genome establish unique epigenomic signatures of neuronal cell types (Qian et al., 2017; Luo et al., 2017; Mo et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work (Qian et al., 2017; Luo et al., 2017; Mo et al., 2015).

claim: In the Dnmt3a cKO model, Dnmt3a is functionally ablated in excitatory neurons in the neocortex and hippocampus starting in mid-to-late gestation (embryonic day E13–15).
source: In this conditional knockout (cKO), Dnmt3a is functionally ablated in excitatory neurons in the neocortex and hippocampus starting in mid-to-late gestation (embryonic day E13–15) (Goebbels et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous characterization of the Nex-Cre mouse line (Goebbels et al., 2006) and confirmed by experimental data (Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 3A).

claim: In Dnmt3a cKO animals, DNA methylation was substantially disrupted in excitatory neurons.
source: In Dnmt3a cKO animals, DNA methylation was substantially disrupted in excitatory neurons, leading to altered behavior and synaptic physiology without early life lethality or overt brain morphological alterations.
evidence: This claim is supported by MethylC-seq data showing reduced DNA methylation (Figure 3C).

claim: Dnmt3a cKO led to altered behavior without early life lethality or overt brain morphological alterations.
source: In Dnmt3a cKO animals, DNA methylation was substantially disrupted in excitatory neurons, leading to altered behavior and synaptic physiology without early life lethality or overt brain morphological alterations.
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data (Figure 1C-E) and histological analysis (Figure 1—figure supplement 3C).

claim: Dnmt3a cKO led to altered synaptic physiology without early life lethality or overt brain morphological alterations.
source: In Dnmt3a cKO animals, DNA methylation was substantially disrupted in excitatory neurons, leading to altered behavior and synaptic physiology without early life lethality or overt brain morphological alterations.
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data (Figure 2E-I) and histological analysis (Figure 1—figure supplement 3C).

claim: The polycomb repressive complex 2 (PRC2)-associated chromatin modification, H3K27me3, increases during postnatal development following the loss of mCH DNA methylation in Dnmt3a cKO neurons primarily at sites where mCG is also depleted.
source: We found that the polycomb repressive complex 2 (PRC2)-associated chromatin modification, H3K27me3, increases during postnatal development following the loss of mCH DNA methylation in Dnmt3a cKO neurons primarily at sites where mCG is also depleted.
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP-seq data showing increased H3K27me3 at sites with reduced DNA methylation (Figure 4B-C, Figure 5A-E).

claim: Neurod6 expression begins between embryonic day E11 and E13.
source: Here, we took a targeted approach by functionally ablating Dnmt3a in cortical pyramidal cells starting during mid-gestation (Figure 1A). We took advantage of the developmental onset of Neurod6 expression between embryonic day E11 and E13, after the onset of Nestin expression (Thompson et al., 2014) but well before the major postnatal wave of reprogramming of the neuronal DNA methylome (Figure 1—figure supplement 1; Lister et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work (Thompson et al., 2014) and in situ hybridization data (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).

claim: Neurod6-dependent Cre recombination occurred only in excitatory neurons.
source: We confirmed that Neurod6-dependent Cre recombination occurred only in excitatory neurons using the INTACT (isolation of nuclei tagged in specific cell types) (Mo et al., 2015) mouse (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data using the INTACT mouse line (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).

claim: The deletion of Dnmt3a exon 19 was faithfully captured in cortical excitatory neurons of cKO animals.
source: The deletion of Dnmt3a exon 19 was faithfully captured in cortical excitatory neurons of cKO animals (Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 3A), which was known to produce a deletion of 50 amino acids in the methyltransferase domain of the DNMT3A protein (Lyko, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data (Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 3A) and citation to previous work (Lyko, 2018).

claim: Deletion of Dnmt3a exon 19 produces a deletion of 50 amino acids in the methyltransferase domain of the DNMT3A protein.
source: The deletion of Dnmt3a exon 19 was faithfully captured in cortical excitatory neurons of cKO animals (Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 3A), which was known to produce a deletion of 50 amino acids in the methyltransferase domain of the DNMT3A protein (Lyko, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work (Lyko, 2018).

claim: DNMT3A protein was reduced in whole tissue extracts at early postnatal time points (P5 and P13) in Dnmt3a cKO animals.
source: We also verified the reduction in DNMT3A protein in whole tissue extracts at early postnatal time points (P5 and P13) when Dnmt3a mediated accumulation of mCH normally begins in the frontal cortex (Lister et al., 2013; Figure 1—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B).

claim: Dnmt3a mediated accumulation of mCH normally begins in the frontal cortex at early postnatal time points (P5 and P13).
source: We also verified the reduction in DNMT3A protein in whole tissue extracts at early postnatal time points (P5 and P13) when Dnmt3a mediated accumulation of mCH normally begins in the frontal cortex (Lister et al., 2013; Figure 1—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work (Lister et al., 2013).

claim: Dnmt3a cKO animals survived and bred normally.
source: Dnmt3a cKO animals survived and bred normally, without overt morphological alterations in the brain (Figure 1—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by observational data from animal husbandry.

claim: Dnmt3a cKO animals had no overt morphological alterations in the brain.
source: Dnmt3a cKO animals survived and bred normally, without overt morphological alterations in the brain (Figure 1—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by histological analysis (Figure 1—figure supplement 3C).

claim: Dnmt3a cKO mice had no impairments in gross motor function in an open field test.
source: We found no impairments in gross motor function in an open field test: cKO mice traveled more during the first 5 min of testing (Figure 1—figure supplement 4A) while performing fewer rearings associated with exploratory interest (Figure 1—figure supplement 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data from open field tests (Figure 1—figure supplement 4A-B).

claim: Dnmt3a cKO mice traveled more during the first 5 min of open field testing.
source: We found no impairments in gross motor function in an open field test: cKO mice traveled more during the first 5 min of testing (Figure 1—figure supplement 4A) while performing fewer rearings associated with exploratory interest (Figure 1—figure supplement 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data from open field tests (Figure 1—figure supplement 4A).

claim: Dnmt3a cKO mice performed fewer rearings associated with exploratory interest in the open field test.
source: We found no impairments in gross motor function in an open field test: cKO mice traveled more during the first 5 min of testing (Figure 1—figure supplement 4A) while performing fewer rearings associated with exploratory interest (Figure 1—figure supplement 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data from open field tests (Figure 1—figure supplement 4B).

claim: Dnmt3a cKO mice had no signs of increased anxiety-like behavior on three separate behavioral tests.
source: Moreover, cKO mice had no signs of increased anxiety-like behavior on three separate behavioral tests (Figure 1—figure supplement 4C-E), in contrast with the reported anxiogenic effects of Dnmt3a knockdown in the mPFC of adult mice (Elliott et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data from anxiety tests (Figure 1—figure supplement 4C-E).

claim: Dnmt3a knockdown in the mPFC of adult mice has anxiogenic effects.
source: Moreover, cKO mice had no signs of increased anxiety-like behavior on three separate behavioral tests (Figure 1—figure supplement 4C-E), in contrast with the reported anxiogenic effects of Dnmt3a knockdown in the mPFC of adult mice (Elliott et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work (Elliott et al., 2016).

claim: Dnmt3a cKO mice made fewer spontaneous alternations in the Y-maze test of working memory.
source: Dnmt3a cKO mice did not alternate spontaneously between the arms of a Y-maze (p=0.0079 for males, p=0.011 for females, Figure 1C), indicating impaired spatial working memory.
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data from Y-maze tests (Figure 1C).

claim: Male Dnmt3a cKO animals spent less time interacting with a novel mouse in the three-chamber test.
source: Moreover, when tested in a three-chamber box in which one of the sides contained a novel mouse and the opposite a novel object, male Dnmt3a cKO animals spent less time in the former, opting, instead, to remain significantly longer in the center (empty compartment), which is suggestive of reduced exploration and social interest (Figure 1D, left panel; p=0.01048).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data from three-chamber sociability tests (Figure 1D).

claim: Male Dnmt3a cKO mice had significantly attenuated acoustic startle reflex.
source: Male Dnmt3a cKO mice also had significantly attenuated acoustic startle reflex (p=0.0019, Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data from acoustic startle tests (Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 5A).

claim: Male Dnmt3a cKO mice showed increased prepulse inhibition (PPI).
source: We observed increased prepulse inhibition (PPI) in male Dnmt3a cKO mice, but this may be driven by the reduced startle reflex (Figure 1—figure supplement 5B, p<0.05).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data from PPI tests (Figure 1—figure supplement 5B).

claim: The increased prepulse inhibition (PPI) in male Dnmt3a cKO mice may be driven by the reduced startle reflex.
source: We observed increased prepulse inhibition (PPI) in male Dnmt3a cKO mice, but this may be driven by the reduced startle reflex (Figure 1—figure supplement 5B, p<0.05).
evidence: This claim is speculative reasoning based on the observed data.

claim: The observed deficits in startle response in Dnmt3a cKO mice were not due to impaired hearing.
source: It is noteworthy that the observed deficits in startle response were not due to impaired hearing, since Dnmt3a cKO mice displayed intact hearing in tests of PPI and fear conditioning.
evidence: This claim is inferred from behavioral data showing intact responses in PPI and fear conditioning tests.

claim: There were no significant differences between Dnmt3a cKO and control male mice in acquisition or recall of fear memory following re-exposure to the context or conditioned stimulus after 24–48 hr.
source: There were no significant differences between Dnmt3a cKO and control male mice in acquisition or recall of fear memory following re-exposure to the context or conditioned stimulus after 24–48 hr (Figure 1—figure supplement 5C-E), or in extinction (Figure 1—figure supplement 5F).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data from fear conditioning tests (Figure 1—figure supplement 5C-F).

claim: There were no significant differences between Dnmt3a cKO and control male mice in extinction of fear memory.
source: There were no significant differences between Dnmt3a cKO and control male mice in acquisition or recall of fear memory following re-exposure to the context or conditioned stimulus after 24–48 hr (Figure 1—figure supplement 5C-E), or in extinction (Figure 1—figure supplement 5F).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data from fear conditioning tests (Figure 1—figure supplement 5F).

claim: The overall density of dendritic spines was equivalent in control and Dnmt3a cKO neurons.
source: While the overall density of dendritic spines was equivalent in control and Dnmt3a cKO neurons (Figure 2B), the spines were significantly longer (mean length 2.219±0.052 µm in cKO, 1.852±0.034 µm in control) and narrower (mean width 0.453±0.008 µm in cKO, 0.519±0.008 µm in control) in Dnmt3a cKO neurons (Figure 2C, KS test p<0.001; Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by morphological analysis of dendritic spines (Figure 2B).

claim: Dendritic spines were significantly longer in Dnmt3a cKO neurons compared to control.
source: While the overall density of dendritic spines was equivalent in control and Dnmt3a cKO neurons (Figure 2B), the spines were significantly longer (mean length 2.219±0.052 µm in cKO, 1.852±0.034 µm in control) and narrower (mean width 0.453±0.008 µm in cKO, 0.519±0.008 µm in control) in Dnmt3a cKO neurons (Figure 2C, KS test p<0.001; Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by morphological analysis of dendritic spines (Figure 2C).

claim: Dendritic spines were significantly narrower in Dnmt3a cKO neurons compared to control.
source: While the overall density of dendritic spines was equivalent in control and Dnmt3a cKO neurons (Figure 2B), the spines were significantly longer (mean length 2.219±0.052 µm in cKO, 1.852±0.034 µm in control) and narrower (mean width 0.453±0.008 µm in cKO, 0.519±0.008 µm in control) in Dnmt3a cKO neurons (Figure 2C, KS test p<0.001; Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by morphological analysis of dendritic spines (Figure 2C).

claim: A larger proportion of spines in Dnmt3a cKO mice were classified as immature filopodia.
source: Consistent with this, a larger proportion of spines in Dnmt3a cKO mice were classified as immature filopodia, and fewer were mushroom-shaped mature spines (Figure 2D) according to pre-established morphometric criteria (see Materials and methods).
evidence: This claim is supported by morphological classification of dendritic spines (Figure 2D).

claim: Fewer spines in Dnmt3a cKO mice were mushroom-shaped mature spines.
source: Consistent with this, a larger proportion of spines in Dnmt3a cKO mice were classified as immature filopodia, and fewer were mushroom-shaped mature spines (Figure 2D) according to pre-established morphometric criteria (see Materials and methods).
evidence: This claim is supported by morphological classification of dendritic spines (Figure 2D).

claim: Dnmt3a cKO neurons required greater current injections than control to trigger an action potential (higher rheobase).
source: Whole-cell current-clamp recordings showed that Dnmt3a cKO neurons (n=22 cells from 11 mice) required greater current injections than control (n=17 cells from 12 mice) to trigger an action potential (higher rheobase, t-test p=0.0042, Figure 2F), though there was no difference in membrane potential at the firing threshold (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data from patch-clamp recordings (Figure 2F).

claim: There was no difference in membrane potential at the firing threshold between Dnmt3a cKO and control neurons.
source: Whole-cell current-clamp recordings showed that Dnmt3a cKO neurons (n=22 cells from 11 mice) required greater current injections than control (n=17 cells from 12 mice) to trigger an action potential (higher rheobase, t-test p=0.0042, Figure 2F), though there was no difference in membrane potential at the firing threshold (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data from patch-clamp recordings (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).

claim: Dnmt3a cKO neurons produced fewer spikes in response to injected current.
source: Dnmt3a cKO neurons also produced fewer spikes in response to injected current (Figure 2G).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data from patch-clamp recordings (Figure 2G).

claim: Dnmt3a cKO neurons were slightly hyperpolarized at rest.
source: These neurons were slightly hyperpolarized at rest (mean –70.90±0.8 mV in cKO, n=22 cells from 11 mice vs. –67.22±1.4 mV in control, n=17 cells from 12 mice, Wilcoxon test p=0.049, Figure 2H), which could reflect differential expression of ion channels at the plasma membrane.
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data from patch-clamp recordings (Figure 2H).

claim: The hyperpolarization at rest in Dnmt3a cKO neurons could reflect differential expression of ion channels at the plasma membrane.
source: These neurons were slightly hyperpolarized at rest (mean –70.90±0.8 mV in cKO, n=22 cells from 11 mice vs. –67.22±1.4 mV in control, n=17 cells from 12 mice, Wilcoxon test p=0.049, Figure 2H), which could reflect differential expression of ion channels at the plasma membrane.
evidence: This claim is speculative reasoning based on the observed electrophysiological data.

claim: Dnmt3a cKO neurons had a lower input resistance.
source: Consistent with this, Dnmt3a cKO neurons had a lower input resistance (Wilcoxon test p=0.023, Figure 2I), suggesting increased expression of functional transmembrane ion channels.
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data from patch-clamp recordings (Figure 2I).

claim: Lower input resistance in Dnmt3a cKO neurons suggests increased expression of functional transmembrane ion channels.
source: Consistent with this, Dnmt3a cKO neurons had a lower input resistance (Wilcoxon test p=0.023, Figure 2I), suggesting increased expression of functional transmembrane ion channels.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the electrophysiological data.

claim: Dnmt3a cKO mice showed slight, yet significant, increased amplitude variability in miniature excitatory postsynaptic currents (mEPSCs).
source: Whole-cell voltage-clamp recordings of miniature excitatory postsynaptic currents (mEPSCs) showed slight, yet significant, increased amplitude variability in Dnmt3a cKO mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 2, 8.77±0.32 pA in cKO, n=8 cells from 4 mice vs. 8.67±0.089 pA in control, n=8 cells from 5 mice, F-test, p=0.0032), consistent with disruption at postsynaptic sites.
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data from voltage-clamp recordings (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B).

claim: Increased amplitude variability in mEPSCs in Dnmt3a cKO mice is consistent with disruption at postsynaptic sites.
source: Whole-cell voltage-clamp recordings of miniature excitatory postsynaptic currents (mEPSCs) showed slight, yet significant, increased amplitude variability in Dnmt3a cKO mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 2, 8.77±0.32 pA in cKO, n=8 cells from 4 mice vs. 8.67±0.089 pA in control, n=8 cells from 5 mice, F-test, p=0.0032), consistent with disruption at postsynaptic sites.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the electrophysiological data.

claim: There was no alteration in the mean amplitude of mEPSCs recorded at the soma in Dnmt3a cKO mice.
source: However, we found no alteration in the mean amplitude (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B) or frequency (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C) of mEPSCs recorded at the soma.
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data from voltage-clamp recordings (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B).

claim: There was no alteration in the frequency of mEPSCs recorded at the soma in Dnmt3a cKO mice.
source: However, we found no alteration in the mean amplitude (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B) or frequency (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C) of mEPSCs recorded at the soma.
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data from voltage-clamp recordings (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C).

claim: Nuclear RNA abundance was highly consistent across independent replicates within the same group (Spearman correlation r=0.93–0.94).
source: Nuclear RNA abundance was highly consistent across independent replicates within the same group (Spearman correlation r=0.93–0.94, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis of RNA-seq data (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).

claim: 46 differentially expressed (DE) genes had higher expression in the Dnmt3a cKO (false discovery rate [FDR] < 0.05).
source: Consistent with this, we detected 46 differentially expressed (DE) genes with higher expression in the cKO (false discovery rate [FDR] < 0.05, Figure 3A–B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data analysis (Figure 3A-B and Supplementary file 2).

claim: 24 genes had significantly lower expression in Dnmt3a cKO neurons.
source: We also detected significantly lower expression of 24 genes in cKO neurons (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data analysis (Figure 3A and Supplementary file 2).

claim: Several of the DE genes had annotated roles in dendrite morphogenesis (Elavl4, Hecw2, Ptprd).
source: Several of the DE genes had annotated roles in dendrite morphogenesis (Elavl4, Hecw2, Ptprd), as well as in the regulation of Na+ (Hecw2, Scn3b) and Ca2+ levels (Cacnb3) (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about gene functions from annotations.

claim: Several of the DE genes had annotated roles in the regulation of Na+ (Hecw2, Scn3b).
source: Several of the DE genes had annotated roles in dendrite morphogenesis (Elavl4, Hecw2, Ptprd), as well as in the regulation of Na+ (Hecw2, Scn3b) and Ca2+ levels (Cacnb3) (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about gene functions from annotations.

claim: Several of the DE genes had annotated roles in the regulation of Ca2+ levels (Cacnb3).
source: Several of the DE genes had annotated roles in dendrite morphogenesis (Elavl4, Hecw2, Ptprd), as well as in the regulation of Na+ (Hecw2, Scn3b) and Ca2+ levels (Cacnb3) (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about gene functions from annotations.

claim: No significant changes in transposable element expression were found between cKO and control in the cortical excitatory neurons (two-sample t-test, FDR > 0.05).
source: We examined the expression of transposon families or classes in our data but found no significant changes between cKO and control in the cortical excitatory neurons (two-sample t-test, FDR > 0.05; Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of transposable element expression (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).

claim: Non-CG DNA methylation (mCH) is absent at birth (<0.1% of all CH sites at P0).
source: Using single base resolution, whole-genome MethylC-seq (Lister et al., 2008) in biological replicates with strong consistency (Figure 3—figure supplement 3A), we confirmed that non-CG DNA methylation (mCH) in excitatory neurons is absent at birth (<0.1% of all CH sites at P0), and accumulates by postnatal day 39 (1.98% at P39) (Lister et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by MethylC-seq data (Figure 3C) and citation to previous work (Lister et al., 2013).

claim: Non-CG DNA methylation (mCH) accumulates by postnatal day 39 (1.98% at P39) in excitatory neurons.
source: Using single base resolution, whole-genome MethylC-seq (Lister et al., 2008) in biological replicates with strong consistency (Figure 3—figure supplement 3A), we confirmed that non-CG DNA methylation (mCH) in excitatory neurons is absent at birth (<0.1% of all CH sites at P0), and accumulates by postnatal day 39 (1.98% at P39) (Lister et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by MethylC-seq data (Figure 3C) and citation to previous work (Lister et al., 2013).

claim: The cKO all but eliminated mCH (<0.1% at P0 and P39).
source: The cKO all but eliminated mCH (<0.1% at P0 and P39) (Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by MethylC-seq data (Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 3B).

claim: The genome-wide mCG level was 12.5% lower in mature (P39) cKO neurons (60.1% in cKO vs. 72.6% in control).
source: While mCH increases in neurons during postnatal life, the genome-wide level of mCG in the brain remains high throughout the lifespan (Lister et al., 2013). We found that the genome-wide mCG level was 12.5% lower in mature (P39) cKO neurons (60.1% in cKO vs. 72.6% in control).
evidence: This claim is supported by MethylC-seq data (Figure 3C).

claim: There was no difference in mCG in newborn mice (P0, 73.1% in both cKO and control).
source: There was no difference in mCG in newborn mice (P0, 73.1% in both cKO and control, Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by MethylC-seq data (Figure 3C).

claim: mCG at P39 was reduced in 92.2% of all genomic bins (10 kb resolution).
source: mCG at P39 was reduced in 92.2% of all genomic bins (10 kb resolution), and was significantly lower in introns, 3' UTR, and intergenic regions (Figure 3—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by MethylC-seq data analysis (Figure 3—figure supplement 3C).

claim: mCG at P39 was significantly lower in introns, 3' UTR, and intergenic regions in Dnmt3a cKO neurons.
source: mCG at P39 was reduced in 92.2% of all genomic bins (10 kb resolution), and was significantly lower in introns, 3' UTR, and intergenic regions (Figure 3—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by MethylC-seq data analysis (Figure 3—figure supplement 3C).

claim: The reduction in mCG was strongly correlated with reduced mCH (Spearman correlation r=0.805, p<10–3).
source: The reduction in mCG was strongly correlated with reduced mCH (Spearman correlation r=0.805, p<10–3, Figure 3—figure supplement 3D).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis of MethylC-seq data (Figure 3—figure supplement 3D).

claim: mCH was strongly enriched in the gene body of up-regulated genes in control neurons.
source: Consistent with this, we found that mCH was strongly enriched in the gene body of up-regulated genes in control neurons (Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of DNA methylation patterns around DE genes (Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 4A).

claim: Genes with similar expression levels in the control neurons which were not transcriptionally up-regulated in the cKO had significantly lower gene body mCH.
source: By contrast, genes with similar expression levels in the control neurons which were not transcriptionally up-regulated in the cKO (Figure 3—figure supplement 4B) had significantly lower gene body mCH (Figure 3D).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of DNA methylation patterns around DE genes (Figure 3D).

claim: Down-regulated genes had low gene body mCH.
source: Moreover, down-regulated genes had low gene body mCH.
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of DNA methylation patterns around DE genes (Figure 3D).

claim: The relatively lower mCH level in down-regulated genes could make them less sensitive to the loss of Dnmt3a.
source: The relatively lower mCH level in down-regulated genes could make them less sensitive to the loss of Dnmt3a.
evidence: This claim is speculative reasoning based on the observed data.

claim: The dysregulation of down-regulated gene expression may be due to secondary effects subsequent to the direct loss of DNA methylation.
source: The dysregulation of their expression may be due to secondary effects subsequent to the direct loss of DNA methylation.
evidence: This claim is speculative reasoning based on the observed data.

claim: mCG was not significantly different between DE and control genes at the promoter and gene body.
source: We also examined the pattern of mCG at the promoter and gene body of DE genes. In contrast with the pattern of mCH, mCG was not significantly different between DE and control genes (Figure 3—figure supplement 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of DNA methylation patterns around DE genes (Figure 3—figure supplement 4C).

claim: The difference in gene body methylation (cKO – control) was negatively correlated with gene expression changes.
source: The difference in gene body methylation (cKO – control) was negatively correlated with gene expression changes, consistent with repressive regulation (Gabel et al., 2015; Lavery et al., 2020; Figure 3E).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis (Figure 3E) and citations to previous work (Gabel et al., 2015; Lavery et al., 2020).

claim: The correlation between gene body methylation difference and gene expression changes accounted for 0.46% of the variance of differential gene expression.
source: This correlation accounted for 0.46% of the variance of differential gene expression, whereas the total explainable variance (R2 between biological replicates) was 1.30% (Figure 3—figure supplement 4D).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the correlation (Figure 3—figure supplement 4D).

claim: Up-regulated genes were on average longer than down-regulated genes (Wilcoxon rank-sum test p<10–4).
source: Up-regulated genes were on average longer than down-regulated genes (Figure 3—figure supplement 4E, Wilcoxon rank-sum test p<10–4) and non-DE genes (p<0.01), consistent with the reported enrichment of mCA and MeCP2-dependent gene repression in long genes (Boxer et al., 2020; Gabel et al., 2015; Kinde et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of gene lengths (Figure 3—figure supplement 4E) and citations to previous work (Boxer et al., 2020; Gabel et al., 2015; Kinde et al., 2016).

claim: Up-regulated genes were on average longer than non-DE genes (p<0.01).
source: Up-regulated genes were on average longer than down-regulated genes (Figure 3—figure supplement 4E, Wilcoxon rank-sum test p<10–4) and non-DE genes (p<0.01), consistent with the reported enrichment of mCA and MeCP2-dependent gene repression in long genes (Boxer et al., 2020; Gabel et al., 2015; Kinde et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of gene lengths (Figure 3—figure supplement 4E) and citations to previous work (Boxer et al., 2020; Gabel et al., 2015; Kinde et al., 2016).

claim: A limited number of DMRs were found in newborn mice (P0: 1087 DMRs with lower, 164 with higher mCG in cKO; ≥30 difference in %mCG; FDR < 0.01).
source: We found a limited number of DMRs in newborn mice (P0: 1087 DMRs with lower, 164 with higher mCG in cKO; ≥30 difference in %mCG; FDR < 0.01).
evidence: This claim is supported by DMR analysis of MethylC-seq data (Supplementary file 3).

claim: 222,006 DMRs with substantially lower mCG in cKO compared with controls were found in mature neurons (P39).
source: In mature neurons (P39), by contrast, we found 222,006 DMRs with substantially lower mCG in cKO compared with controls (Figure 3—figure supplement 5A; Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by DMR analysis of MethylC-seq data (Figure 3—figure supplement 5A and Supplementary file 3).

claim: Only 89 DMRs had ≥30 higher %mCG in cKO at P39.
source: Only 89 DMRs had ≥30 higher %mCG in cKO.
evidence: This claim is supported by DMR analysis of MethylC-seq data (Supplementary file 3).

claim: Five DMRs were found in an approximately 40 kb region around the promoter of the DE gene Nedd4.
source: To illustrate, we found five DMRs in an ~40 kb region around the promoter of the DE gene Nedd4 (Figure 3F).
evidence: This claim is supported by visualization of DMRs at the Nedd4 locus (Figure 3F).

claim: Four of the five P39 Dnmt3a cKO DMRs at the Nedd4 locus were also unmethylated in excitatory neurons in newborn mice.
source: Four of these DMRs were also unmethylated in excitatory neurons in newborn mice, showing that the loss of Dnmt3a blocked the developmental gain of mCG at these sites.
evidence: This claim is supported by visualization of DMRs at the Nedd4 locus (Figure 3F).

claim: The loss of Dnmt3a blocked the developmental gain of mCG at four DMRs at the Nedd4 locus.
source: Four of these DMRs were also unmethylated in excitatory neurons in newborn mice, showing that the loss of Dnmt3a blocked the developmental gain of mCG at these sites.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the comparison of methylation levels at different developmental stages (Figure 3F).

claim: The density of P39 cKO DMRs around the DE genes was not significantly different in the up- and down-regulated genes and the non-DE genes.
source: However, the density of P39 cKO DMRs around the DE genes was not significantly different in the up- and down-regulated genes and the non-DE genes (Figure 3—figure supplement 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of DMR density around genes (Figure 3—figure supplement 5B).

claim: The majority of P39 cKO DMRs (68.0%) were distal (≥10 kb) from the annotated transcription start sites.
source: The majority of P39 cKO DMRs (68.0%) were distal (≥10 kb) from the annotated transcription start sites.
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of DMR locations relative to genes.

claim: P39 cKO DMRs were significantly enriched in both active enhancers and repressed chromatin.
source: These DMRs were significantly enriched in both active enhancers and repressed chromatin, suggesting they have a regulatory role (Figure 3—figure supplement 5C; see also below).
evidence: This claim is supported by enrichment analysis of DMRs in chromatin states (Figure 3—figure supplement 5C).

claim: 113,557 developmental DMRs that gain mCG between P0 and P39 in control neurons were found (≥30 difference in %mCG, FDR < 0.01).
source: We found 113,557 developmental DMRs that gain mCG between P0 and P39 in control neurons (≥30 difference in %mCG, FDR < 0.01).
evidence: This claim is supported by DMR analysis comparing P0 and P39 control samples (Supplementary file 3).

claim: Developmental DMRs strongly overlapped (83.2%) with the cKO DMRs in mature neurons.
source: These DMRs strongly overlapped (83.2%) with the cKO DMRs in mature neurons (Figure 3G–H, Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by overlap analysis of DMRs (Figure 3G-H and Supplementary file 3).

claim: P39 cKO DMRs were enriched in DNA sequence motifs of multiple transcription factors (TFs) associated with neuronal differentiation, including Rest, Lhx2, Pou3f2(Brn2), and Pax6 (FDR < 0.05).
source: Moreover, the P39 cKO DMRs were enriched in DNA sequence motifs of multiple transcription factors (TFs) associated with neuronal differentiation, including Rest, Lhx2, Pou3f2(Brn2), and Pax6 (FDR < 0.05, Figure 3—figure supplement 5D, Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by motif enrichment analysis (Figure 3—figure supplement 5D and Supplementary file 4).

claim: The DMRs in Dnmt3a cKO neurons represent only a part of the global reduction in mCG that was observed throughout the genome.
source: Notably, the DMRs in Dnmt3a cKO neurons represent only a part of the global reduction in mCG that we observed throughout the genome.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that mCG is reduced by approximately 10% in all genomic compartments, even after excluding P39 DMRs.

claim: mCG is reduced by approximately 10% in all genomic compartments, even after excluding P39 DMRs.
source: Indeed, we found that mCG is reduced by ~10% in all genomic compartments, even after excluding P39 DMRs (Figure 3—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of mCG levels in genomic compartments (Figure 3—figure supplement 3C).

claim: Dnmt3a is essential for the methylation and subsequent repression of neuronal enhancers that are active during prenatal brain development.
source: These results suggest that Dnmt3a is essential for the methylation and subsequent repression of neuronal enhancers that are active during prenatal brain development.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the enrichment of DMRs in enhancers and their overlap with developmental DMRs.

claim: Chromatin regulators associated with PRC2, including Ezh2, Suz12, Eed, and Jarid2, were among the top DNA binding proteins enriched near the promoters of both up- and down-regulated DE genes.
source: Chromatin regulators associated with PRC2, including Ezh2, Suz12, Eed, and Jarid2, were among the top DNA binding proteins enriched near the promoters of both up- and down-regulated DE genes (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by BART analysis (Figure 4A and Supplementary file 5).

claim: Several TFs associated with chromatin organization, including the histone deacetylase (Hdac) and demethylase (Kdm) families, and Ctcf, were enriched near the promoters of DE genes.
source: Several TFs associated with chromatin organization, including the histone deacetylase (Hdac) and demethylase (Kdm) families, and Ctcf, were also enriched (Figure 4—figure supplement 1, Supplementary file 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by BART analysis (Figure 4—figure supplement 1 and Supplementary file 5).

claim: Dnmt3a cKO impacts the chromatin landscape in excitatory neurons, potentially via altered PRC2 activity.
source: These results suggest that Dnmt3a cKO impacts the chromatin landscape in excitatory neurons, potentially via altered PRC2 activity.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the enrichment of PRC2-associated factors near DE genes.

claim: Increased H3K27me3 at the Mab21l2 locus coincides with the loss of DNA methylation in P39 Dnmt3a cKO.
source: Browser view of the Mab21l2 locus, where increased H3K27me3 (differentially modified regions, bottom red bars and highlighted in blue shaded box) coincides with the loss of DNA methylation (Dnmt3a cKO DMRs, orange bars under the 'P39 cKO' track and highlighted in blue shaded box) in P39 Dnmt3a cKO.
evidence: This claim is supported by visualization of ChIP-seq and MethylC-seq data at the Mab21l2 locus (Figure 4B).

claim: The Mab21l2 locus loses H3K27me3 during normal development in control pyramidal neurons (P39 < E14).
source: This region loses H3K27me3 during normal development in control pyramidal neurons (blue bars, P39 < E14).
evidence: This claim is supported by visualization of ChIP-seq data at the Mab21l2 locus (Figure 4B).

claim: There was a 2.41-fold increase in H3K27me3 at the Mab21l2 locus in P39 Dnmt3a cKO neurons (FDR = 1.33e-4).
source: Quantification of the increase in H3K27me3 chromatin immunoprecipitation sequencing (ChIP-seq) signal in each replicate at the H3K27me3 differentially modified region between P39 control and cKO at the Mab21l2 locus shown in (B). Each bar shows the DEseq2 normalized counts in each replicate, and the triple asterisks denote a significant increase (false discovery rate [FDR] = 1.33e-4, fold-change=2.41).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification of ChIP-seq signal (Figure 4C).

claim: The Mab21l2 gene was lowly expressed (TPM < 3) in both control and cKO neurons.
source: The Mab21l2 gene was lowly expressed (TPM < 3) in both control and cKO neurons, consistent with a role for the gain of H3K27me3 in maintaining the repression of this gene.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data.

claim: The gain of H3K27me3 at the Mab21l2 locus is consistent with a role in maintaining the repression of this gene.
source: The Mab21l2 gene was lowly expressed (TPM < 3) in both control and cKO neurons, consistent with a role for the gain of H3K27me3 in maintaining the repression of this gene.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that the gene remains lowly expressed despite loss of DNA methylation.

claim: Marks associated with transcriptional activity (H3K4me3 and H3K27ac) were largely conserved in the P39 cKO and control.
source: Using a conservative strategy to call ChIP-seq peaks (Zang et al., 2009), we found that marks associated with transcriptional activity (H3K4me3 and H3K27ac) were largely conserved in the P39 cKO and control (Figure 4D).
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP-seq peak analysis (Figure 4D).

claim: 51.9% more H3K27me3 peaks were found in mature (P39) cKO than in control neurons.
source: By contrast, we found 51.9% more H3K27me3 peaks in mature (P39) cKO than in control neurons (Figure 4D, Supplementary file 6).
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP-seq peak analysis (Figure 4D and Supplementary file 6).

claim: No differentially modified (DM) regions for H3K4me3 and H3K27ac were found between the cKO and control in P39 neurons.
source: When we directly identified differentially modified (DM) regions, we found no DM for H3K4me3 and H3K27ac between the cKO and control in P39 neurons (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by differential binding analysis of ChIP-seq data (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).

claim: 4040 regions with significantly increased H3K27me3 in the P39 cKO were found, covering approximately 31.05 MB of the genome (FDR < 0.05).
source: By contrast, we found 4040 regions with significantly increased H3K27me3 in the P39 cKO, covering ~31.05 MB of the genome (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D, FDR < 0.05, Supplementary file 7).
evidence: This claim is supported by differential binding analysis of ChIP-seq data (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D and Supplementary file 7).

claim: Only 3 DM regions were found in earlier development stages (E14 or P0).
source: Differential H3K27me3 appears late during brain maturation: only 3 DM regions were found in earlier development stages (E14 or P0; Figure 4—figure supplement 1D), and the signal differences of cKO and control did not show clear correlations between P39 and earlier stages (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by differential binding analysis of ChIP-seq data at different developmental stages (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).

claim: The signal differences of cKO and control H3K27me3 did not show clear correlations between P39 and earlier stages.
source: Differential H3K27me3 appears late during brain maturation: only 3 DM regions were found in earlier development stages (E14 or P0; Figure 4—figure supplement 1D), and the signal differences of cKO and control did not show clear correlations between P39 and earlier stages (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis of H3K27me3 signal differences across developmental stages (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).

claim: H3K27me3 DM regions have a medium but non-zero level of H3K27me3 in the P39 control.
source: These DM regions have a medium but non-zero level of H3K27me3 in the P39 control (higher than random shuffles across the whole genome but lower than random shuffles within the peak regions, Figure 4—figure supplement 3A), and hence presumably fine-tunable after Dnmt3a cKO.
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of H3K27me3 signal in DM regions compared to shuffled controls (Figure 4—figure supplement 3A).

claim: H3K27me3 DM regions are presumably fine-tunable after Dnmt3a cKO.
source: These DM regions have a medium but non-zero level of H3K27me3 in the P39 control (higher than random shuffles across the whole genome but lower than random shuffles within the peak regions, Figure 4—figure supplement 3A), and hence presumably fine-tunable after Dnmt3a cKO.
evidence: This claim is speculative reasoning based on the observed H3K27me3 levels.

claim: Genes associated with H3K27me3 DM regions were enriched in development-related functions.
source: Genes associated with these DM regions were enriched in development-related functions (Figure 4—figure supplement 3B, Supplementary file 8).
evidence: This claim is supported by Gene Ontology enrichment analysis (Figure 4—figure supplement 3B and Supplementary file 8).

claim: The increase of H3K27me3 in Dnmt3a cKO excitatory neurons occurred postnatally, following the major impact of the loss of Dnmt3a on neuronal DNA methylation.
source: These results suggest that the increase of H3K27me3 in Dnmt3a cKO excitatory neurons occurred postnatally, following the major impact of the loss of Dnmt3a on neuronal DNA methylation.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the timing of H3K27me3 changes relative to DNA methylation changes.

claim: The majority (66.2%) of the regions marked by H3K27me3 in the cKO overlapped with P39 cKO DMRs (Fisher's test p<1e-100).
source: The increase in H3K27me3 was closely associated with regions that lost CG DNA methylation in the Dnmt3a cKO. The majority (66.2%) of the regions marked by H3K27me3 in the cKO overlapped with P39 cKO DMRs (Figure 5A, Fisher's test p<1e-100).
evidence: This claim is supported by overlap analysis (Figure 5A).

claim: P39 cKO DMRs were significantly enriched in H3K27me3 peaks (22.4% overlapped H3K27me3 peaks in cKO, p<1e-100).
source: Likewise, P39 cKO DMRs were significantly enriched in peaks (22.4% overlapped H3K27me3 peaks in cKO, p<1e-100, Figure 5B) and DM regions of H3K27me3 (Figure 4—figure supplement 3D).
evidence: This claim is supported by enrichment analysis (Figure 5B).

claim: P39 cKO DMRs were significantly enriched in DM regions of H3K27me3.
source: Likewise, P39 cKO DMRs were significantly enriched in peaks (22.4% overlapped H3K27me3 peaks in cKO, p<1e-100, Figure 5B) and DM regions of H3K27me3 (Figure 4—figure supplement 3D).
evidence: This claim is supported by enrichment analysis (Figure 4—figure supplement 3D).

claim: The DM regions of H3K27me3 had significantly more overlaps with DMRs compared to the non-DM control regions (Fisher's exact test p<2.2e-16, OR: 2.70).
source: The DM regions of H3K27me3 had significantly more overlaps with DMRs compared to the non-DM control regions (Fisher's exact test p<2.2e-16, OR: 2.70, Figure 4—figure supplement 3C-D).
evidence: This claim is supported by enrichment analysis (Figure 4—figure supplement 3C-D).

claim: The DM regions have larger decreases in both mCG and mCH when compared to non-DM regions (Wilcoxon rank-sum test p<0.0001).
source: The DM regions also have larger decreases in both mCG and mCH when compared to non-DM regions (Wilcoxon rank-sum test p<0.0001, Figure 4—figure supplement 3E).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of methylation changes in DM and non-DM regions (Figure 4—figure supplement 3E).

claim: DMRs were depleted in regions marked by H3K27ac (12.7%, p<1e-100).
source: Conversely, the DMRs were depleted in regions marked by H3K27ac (12.7%, p<1e-100) or H3K4me3 (0.98%, p=1.73e-149) (Figure 5A–B).
evidence: This claim is supported by enrichment analysis (Figure 5A-B).

claim: DMRs were depleted in regions marked by H3K4me3 (0.98%, p=1.73e-149).
source: Conversely, the DMRs were depleted in regions marked by H3K27ac (12.7%, p<1e-100) or H3K4me3 (0.98%, p=1.73e-149) (Figure 5A–B).
evidence: This claim is supported by enrichment analysis (Figure 5A-B).

claim: H3K27me3 was more abundant at the center of DMRs in cKO compared to control neurons at P39 (∆=0.15 in the unit of fold enrichment vs. IgG, 5.04% increases).
source: Moreover, H3K27me3 was more abundant at the center of DMRs in cKO compared to control neurons at P39 (∆=0.15 in the unit of fold enrichment vs. IgG, 5.04% increases, Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of H3K27me3 signal around DMR centers (Figure 5C).

claim: There were much smaller changes of H3K27me3 at DMRs in newborn (P0, ∆=0.0075, 0.27% changes) or fetal (E14, ∆=–0.028, –1.02% changes) neurons.
source: There were much smaller changes of H3K27me3 at these DMRs in newborn (P0, ∆=0.0075, 0.27% changes) or fetal (E14, ∆=–0.028, –1.02% changes) neurons (Figure 5C), and the increases were not seen in randomly shuffled regions (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of H3K27me3 signal around DMR centers at different developmental stages (Figure 5C).

claim: The increases in H3K27me3 at DMRs were not seen in randomly shuffled regions.
source: There were much smaller changes of H3K27me3 at these DMRs in newborn (P0, ∆=0.0075, 0.27% changes) or fetal (E14, ∆=–0.028, –1.02% changes) neurons (Figure 5C), and the increases were not seen in randomly shuffled regions (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison with shuffled control regions (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).

claim: The signal of H3K4me3 at the DMRs was elevated in the cKO (H3K4me3: ∆=0.068, 2.92% changes).
source: The signal of H3K4me3 and H3K27ac at the DMRs was also elevated in the cKO, to a lesser extent (H3K4me3: ∆=0.068, 2.92% changes; H3K27ac: ∆=0.13, 4.64% changes).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of H3K4me3 signal around DMR centers (Figure 5C).

claim: The signal of H3K27ac at the DMRs was elevated in the cKO (H3K27ac: ∆=0.13, 4.64% changes).
source: The signal of H3K4me3 and H3K27ac at the DMRs was also elevated in the cKO, to a lesser extent (H3K4me3: ∆=0.068, 2.92% changes; H3K27ac: ∆=0.13, 4.64% changes).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of H3K27ac signal around DMR centers (Figure 5C).

claim: At H3K27me3 peaks, the ChIP-seq signal intensity fold-change between cKO and control correlated with the loss of mCG in cKO (Spearman r=–0.26, p<2.2e-16).
source: Going beyond overlaps of regions, we found a quantitative association between the changes in DNA methylation and H3K27me3 in mature (P39) neurons (Figure 5D). At H3K27me3 peaks, the ChIP-seq signal intensity fold-change between cKO and control correlated with the loss of mCG in cKO (Spearman r=–0.26, p<2.2e-16).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis (Figure 5D).

claim: Bigger H3K27me3 increases were observed in genomic bins with overlapping DMRs compared to bins without overlapping DMRs (Wilcoxon rank-sum test p<0.001 in each bin).
source: When accessing the H3K27me3 changes as a function of baseline H3K27me3 levels in the control across the genome tiled in 1 kb bins, we observed bigger H3K27me3 increases in bins with overlapping DMRs compared to bins without overlapping DMRs (Wilcoxon rank-sum test p<0.001 in each bin, Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of H3K27me3 changes stratified by baseline levels (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).

claim: Down-regulated genes that overlap DMRs showed a small but significant median increase of H3K27me3 in the cKO (Wilcoxon rank-sum test p-value < 0.05).
source: We found that down-regulated genes that overlap DMRs and the non-DE genes selected with matched expressions of up-regulated DE genes that overlap DMRs showed a small but significant median increase of H3K27me3 in the cKO (Wilcoxon rank-sum test p-value < 0.05; Figure 5E upper panel).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of H3K27me3 changes in gene bodies (Figure 5E).

claim: Non-DE genes selected with matched expressions of up-regulated DE genes that overlap DMRs showed a small but significant median increase of H3K27me3 in the cKO (Wilcoxon rank-sum test p-value < 0.05).
source: We found that down-regulated genes that overlap DMRs and the non-DE genes selected with matched expressions of up-regulated DE genes that overlap DMRs showed a small but significant median increase of H3K27me3 in the cKO (Wilcoxon rank-sum test p-value < 0.05; Figure 5E upper panel).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of H3K27me3 changes in gene bodies (Figure 5E).

claim: Down-regulated DE genes containing DMRs accumulate significantly more H3K27me3 than non-DE genes containing DMRs and up-regulated genes containing DMRs (Wilcoxon rank-sum test p=0.0029).
source: When we considered a larger set of DE genes with a more relaxed threshold (FDR < 0.2), we observed that down-regulated DE genes containing DMRs accumulate significantly more H3K27me3 than non-DE genes containing DMRs and up-regulated genes containing DMRs (Wilcoxon rank-sum test p=0.0029, Figure 5—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of H3K27me3 changes in gene bodies with a relaxed DE threshold (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A).

claim: Up-regulated genes had no significant accumulation of H3K27me3 and were not significantly different from the control genes.
source: By contrast, up-regulated genes had no significant accumulation of H3K27me3 and were not significantly different from the control genes (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of H3K27me3 changes in gene bodies (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A).

claim: No differences in H3K27me3 were observed between DE and non-DE genes without overlapping DMRs.
source: No such differences were observed between DE and non-DE genes without overlapping DMRs (Figure 5E lower panel and Figure 5—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of H3K27me3 changes in gene bodies (Figure 5E and Figure 5—figure supplement 2A).

claim: The effect of H3K27me3 is likely specific to genes containing DMRs and the effect is stronger in the down-regulated DE genes.
source: These results suggest that the effect of H3K27me3 is likely specific to genes containing DMRs and the effect is stronger in the down-regulated DE genes, which may partially explain the fact that 24 genes were significantly down-regulated after the loss of repressive DNA methylation in the Dnmt3a cKO (Figure 2A–B).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the differential H3K27me3 accumulation in different gene groups.

claim: A larger increase of H3K27me3 signal in the gene body was observed in genes that lost most mCH in the cKO.
source: In all non-DE genes (FDR ≥ 0.05), we observed a larger increase of H3K27me3 signal in the gene body of genes that lost most mCH in the cKO (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of H3K27me3 changes as a function of mCH loss (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B).

claim: Genes that lost the most mCH had a negative correlation between the changes in gene body H3K27me3 signal and gene expression fold-change.
source: Indeed, when we grouped all genes by the extent of the loss of mCH, we found that genes that lost the most mCH had a negative correlation between the changes in gene body H3K27me3 signal and gene expression fold-change. Such correlation was not observed in genes that did not lose mCH (Figure 5—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis stratified by mCH loss (Figure 5—figure supplement 2C).

claim: No correlation between changes in gene body H3K27me3 signal and gene expression fold-change was observed in genes that did not lose mCH.
source: Indeed, when we grouped all genes by the extent of the loss of mCH, we found that genes that lost the most mCH had a negative correlation between the changes in gene body H3K27me3 signal and gene expression fold-change. Such correlation was not observed in genes that did not lose mCH (Figure 5—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis stratified by mCH loss (Figure 5—figure supplement 2C).

claim: H3K27me3 may have a role in repressing expression specifically in regions that lose repressive non-CG DNA methylation.
source: These results suggest that H3K27me3 may have a role in repressing expression specifically in regions that lose repressive non-CG DNA methylation.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the correlation between mCH loss and H3K27me3 gain.

claim: 12,994 developmentally regulated H3K27me3 DM regions between E14 and P39 were identified, with a similar number of regions that gain (6774) and lose (6220) H3K27me3.
source: We identified 12,994 developmentally regulated H3K27me3 DM regions between E14 and P39, with a similar number of regions that gain (6774) and lose (6220) H3K27me3 (Figure 6A and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A, Supplementary file 9).
evidence: This claim is supported by differential binding analysis of ChIP-seq data across developmental stages (Figure 6A and Supplementary file 9).

claim: The developmental H3K27me3 DM regions overlapped developmental DMRs, with a notable overlap of regions gaining both mCG and H3K27me3.
source: The developmental H3K27me3 DM regions overlapped developmental DMRs, with a notable overlap of regions gaining both mCG and H3K27me3 (Figure 6B).
evidence: This claim is supported by overlap analysis (Figure 6B).

claim: Both mCG and H3K27me3 may act together to repress thousands of genomic regions during development.
source: Both modifications may thus act together to repress thousands of genomic regions during development.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the overlap of regions gaining both modifications during development.

claim: The P39 Dnmt3a cKO changes of H3K27me3 signal were weakly correlated with the developmental changes of H3K27me3 signal (r = –0.12, p<2.2e-16).
source: The P39 Dnmt3a cKO changes of H3K27me3 signal were weakly correlated with the developmental changes of H3K27me3 signal (r = –0.12, p<2.2e-16, Figure 6—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C).

claim: There was little appreciable difference between the H3K27me3 signal fold-changes between P39 and E14 cKO samples compared with those of control samples (Spearman r=0.67, p<2.2e-16).
source: Moreover, there was little appreciable difference between the H3K27me3 signal fold-changes between P39 and E14 cKO samples compared with those of control samples (Spearman r=0.67, p<2.2e-16, Figure 6—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis (Figure 6—figure supplement 1D).

claim: Developmental peaks (DevLoss and DevGain) were relatively unaffected by the cKO (ΔH3K27me3=0.02, –0.03 respectively, in units of log10(CPM +1)).
source: We found that developmental peaks (DevLoss and DevGain) were relatively unaffected by the cKO (ΔH3K27me3=0.02, –0.03 respectively, in units of log10(CPM +1)), whereas Group cKO had 4.5-fold larger mean effect (ΔH3K27me3=0.09).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of H3K27me3 changes in different peak groups (Figure 6C-E).

claim: Group cKO peaks had 4.5-fold larger mean effect in H3K27me3 changes (ΔH3K27me3=0.09).
source: We found that developmental peaks (DevLoss and DevGain) were relatively unaffected by the cKO (ΔH3K27me3=0.02, –0.03 respectively, in units of log10(CPM +1)), whereas Group cKO had 4.5-fold larger mean effect (ΔH3K27me3=0.09).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of H3K27me3 changes in different peak groups (Figure 6C-E).

claim: Group cKO peaks experienced greater loss of mCG (ΔmCG = –23.5%) than Group DevLoss (–13.0%) or DevGain (18.6%).
source: Group cKO peaks also experienced greater loss of mCG (ΔmCG = –23.5%) than Group DevLoss (–13.0%) or DevGain (18.6%) (Figure 6C–E and Figure 6—figure supplement 1E-G, middle and right panels).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of methylation changes in different peak groups (Figure 6C-E).

claim: Regions prone to alteration of H3K27me3 by Dnmt3a cKO are distinct from the regions affected by developmentally dynamic H3K27me3.
source: These results suggest that regions prone to alteration of H3K27me3 by Dnmt3a cKO are distinct from the regions affected by developmentally dynamic H3K27me3.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the differential effects on developmental vs. cKO-specific H3K27me3 changes.

claim: More than twice as many DMVs were found in P39 cKO (1838) compared with control (881) neurons.
source: We found more than twice as many DMVs in P39 cKO (1838) compared with control (881) neurons (Supplementary file 10), covering a greater genomic territory (16.02 Mbp in cKO, 7.91 Mbp in control).
evidence: This claim is supported by DMV identification analysis (Supplementary file 10).

claim: P39 cKO DMVs covered a greater genomic territory (16.02 Mbp in cKO, 7.91 Mbp in control).
source: We found more than twice as many DMVs in P39 cKO (1838) compared with control (881) neurons (Supplementary file 10), covering a greater genomic territory (16.02 Mbp in cKO, 7.91 Mbp in control).
evidence: This claim is supported by DMV identification analysis (Supplementary file 10).

claim: The majority of P39 DMVs were either expanded or unique in cKO.
source: The majority of these P39 DMVs were either expanded or unique in cKO (Figure 7A), while DMVs identified in P0 samples were mostly not altered (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by categorization of DMVs (Figure 7A).

claim: DMVs identified in P0 samples were mostly not altered.
source: The majority of these P39 DMVs were either expanded or unique in cKO (Figure 7A), while DMVs identified in P0 samples were mostly not altered (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by categorization of DMVs (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).

claim: Most P39 DMVs had active histone marks (H3K27ac+, H3K27me3-).
source: Most P39 DMVs had active histone marks (H3K27ac+, H3K27me3-), while some had repressed or bivalent profiles consistent with PRC2-associated gene silencing (H3K27me3+) (Figure 7B).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of histone marks at DMVs (Figure 7B).

claim: Some P39 DMVs had repressed or bivalent profiles consistent with PRC2-associated gene silencing (H3K27me3+).
source: Most P39 DMVs had active histone marks (H3K27ac+, H3K27me3-), while some had repressed or bivalent profiles consistent with PRC2-associated gene silencing (H3K27me3+) (Figure 7B).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of histone marks at DMVs (Figure 7B).

claim: Eight distinct categories of DMVs were found by clustering using their pattern of DNA methylation, chromatin modifications, and gene expression.
source: By clustering the DMVs using their pattern of DNA methylation, chromatin modifications, and gene expression, we found eight distinct categories (Figure 7C–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by clustering analysis (Figure 7C).

claim: Cluster C6 DMVs, such as the promoter of Tfap2c, had high H3K27me3 and low mCG in both control and cKO neurons, and were not strongly affected by the loss of mC in the Dnmt3a cKO.
source: Cluster C6 DMVs, such as the promoter of Tfap2c (Figure 7C–D), had high H3K27me3 and low mCG in both control and cKO neurons, and were not strongly affected by the loss of mC in the Dnmt3a cKO.
evidence: This claim is supported by clustering analysis and visualization of specific DMVs (Figure 7C-D).

claim: Cluster C1 and C4 DMVs, including the promoters of Lhx2, Foxp1, Foxp2, Slc17a6 (encoding vesicular glutamate transporter, Vglut2) and Sema3f, gain mC during normal development.
source: By contrast, cluster C1 and C4 DMVs, including the promoters of Lhx2, Foxp1, Foxp2, Slc17a6 (encoding vesicular glutamate transporter, Vglut2) and Sema3f, gain mC during normal development (Figure 7C–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by clustering analysis and visualization of specific DMVs (Figure 7C-D).

claim: Cluster C1 DMVs gained H3K27me3 in the P39 cKO compared to control animals.
source: Cluster C1 DMVs gained H3K27me3 in the P39 cKO compared to control animals.
evidence: This claim is supported by clustering analysis (Figure 7C).

claim: The loss of mC in cluster C1 DMVs in the Dnmt3a cKO did not lead to strong activation of gene expression, potentially due to compensatory PRC2-mediated repression.
source: The loss of mC in these regions in the Dnmt3a cKO did not lead to strong activation of gene expression, potentially due to compensatory PRC2-mediated repression.
evidence: This claim is speculative reasoning based on the observed data.

claim: Cluster C5 DMVs (e.g. Nr1d1, Pde4d) have high mCG at P0 and lose methylation in excitatory neurons during brain development.
source: Cluster C5 DMVs (e.g. Nr1d1, Pde4d, Figure 7D) have high mCG at P0 and lose methylation in excitatory neurons during brain development.
evidence: This claim is supported by clustering analysis and visualization of specific DMVs (Figure 7C-D).

claim: The demethylation of cluster C5 DMVs is not affected in the Dnmt3a cKO.
source: This demethylation is not affected in the Dnmt3a cKO, and we found little difference between the control and cKO neurons at these sites.
evidence: This claim is supported by clustering analysis (Figure 7C).

claim: Clusters C2 and C3 were enriched for up- and down-regulated genes, respectively.
source: Finally, clusters C2 and C3 were enriched for up- and down-regulated genes, respectively.
evidence: This claim is supported by clustering analysis (Figure 7C).

claim: The loss of DNA methylation in excitatory neurons has effects on gene expression, synaptic function, and cognitive behavior.
source: Our findings highlight the critical and interconnected roles in brain development and cognitive function of two major modes of epigenetic repression of gene expression: DNA methylation and PRC2-mediated repression. The loss of DNA methylation in excitatory neurons has effects on gene expression, synaptic function, and cognitive behavior.
evidence: This claim is supported by the combined results from RNA-seq, electrophysiology, and behavioral experiments.

claim: Loss of DNA methylation leads to a gain of the PRC2-associated repressive mark H3K27me3.
source: Moreover, loss of DNA methylation leads to a gain of the PRC2-associated repressive mark H3K27me3.
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP-seq data showing increased H3K27me3 in regions with reduced DNA methylation.

claim: PRC2-mediated repression may compensate for the loss of mCG and/or mCH, acting as an alternative repressive mechanism when DNA methylation is disrupted.
source: PRC2-mediated repression may compensate for the loss of mCG and/or mCH, acting as an alternative repressive mechanism when DNA methylation is disrupted.
evidence: This claim is speculative reasoning based on the observed increase in H3K27me3 following loss of DNA methylation.
